<p class="reading-time">Working paper, draft September 2026 · about 34 min for the main text; exhibits, boundaries and glossary extra</p>

::: {.standfirst}
Two models predict next month's stock returns from 132 measurable company traits. In a typical month their predictions are five parts in a million apart. Feed both to the same portfolio rule and the holdings differ: the gap between the two sets of positions is about 60 percent of the size of the positions themselves <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table V">(Table V)</span>. No new information explains that. A small safety constant does. The rule adds 0.01 to every factor's risk to keep its arithmetic stable, and the two models measure their factors in different units, so the same 0.01 is a different penalty. This matters because research compares forecasts, and a forecast is not a portfolio. A second finding: a piece of expected return that a factor-only portfolio leaves out lifts the Sharpe ratio, return per unit of risk, from 0.39 to 2.51 before any trading costs over 594 months, and by much less after 2007 <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table VII; Section VI.C">(Table VII; Section VI.C)</span>.
:::

[^hero-encoding]: Encoding of the graphic: each dot is one of the three cheapness measures; its position on a ruler is the length that ruler assigns to a unit bet on that measure, so dots that sit apart are counted as separate bets and dots that coincide are counted as one. The plain ruler treats every characteristic as its own axis; the Gram ruler measures the average squared exposure a direction creates across stocks, so measures that pick the same stocks collapse together <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section I.B, equation 3">(Section I.B, equation 3)</span>. The picture is schematic; the paper's measurement of the same idea across 132 characteristics is in Section 6.

## Logic map {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.logic-map}
1. **The question.** When a factor model's forecast becomes a portfolio, how do the units used to measure exposure change what is held? → [The puzzle](#the-puzzle "Abstract; Introduction")
2. **Why it matters.** A forecast is not a portfolio: identical forecasts can produce different holdings for reasons that are not information. → [Why it matters](#why-it-matters "Section III.B; Table V")
3. **The design.** 132 traits, 618 months, three models that differ in one thing at a time: first the ruler, then the intercept. → [How the paper answers it](#how-the-paper-answers-it "Tables I and II; Sections II.A to II.D")
4. **The framework.** The data fix each stock's total expected return; the ruler decides how it is split, and a matched switch changes nothing in fit. → [Where it sits](#where-it-sits "Section I.D, Proposition 1; Section I.C")
5. **A simple example.** Double a factor and halve its loadings: forecast and risk unchanged, but the fixed safety penalty falls to a quarter. → [A simple example](#a-simple-example "Section IV.B, equations 12 to 14")
6. **What the paper finds.** 132 traits behave like about 20; the safety constant, not information, explains the portfolio gap; the left-out return component is worth most of the Sharpe ratio, before costs. → [Results, parts 1 to 3](#results-part-1 "Figure 1; Table V; Figure 2; Table VII")
7. **Prior work and contribution.** Forecasting is well covered; shrinkage and constraints shape positions in stock space; this paper shows the penalty changes with factor units and measures one input's worth inside one fit. → [How this compares](#how-this-compares "Introduction; Section IV.B; Section V")
8. **Practice.** Before reading a change in holdings as new information, check the factor units and the regularisation. → [Why practitioners should care](#why-practitioners-should-care "Section IV.C; Conclusion")
9. **Boundaries.** Gross is not net; a mechanism check is not a performance test; overlap is not a count of priced risks; the intercept effect is weaker after 2007. → [What this paper does not claim](#what-this-paper-does-not-claim "Sections I.C, IV.C, VI.C, VI.D; Tables IV, VI, IA.VI")
:::

## The puzzle: same forecasts, different portfolios {#the-puzzle}

Take two factor models built from the same 132 firm characteristics and the same 618 months of U.S. stock returns <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section II.A">(Section II.A)</span>. A factor is a common source of return that many stocks share; a characteristic is a measurable trait of a company, such as its size or its book-to-market ratio. Both models use three statistical factors and the five Fama-French factors, five published benchmark factors. Their next-month return forecasts agree to about five parts in a million in a typical month: the median relative difference is 4.7 parts per million <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section III.B">(Section III.B)</span>. Hand both forecasts to the same portfolio rule with the same settings. The two portfolios are visibly different books. The median cosine between their weight vectors is 0.83, where 1 means the same direction, and in half the months it lies between 0.75 and 0.88 <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section III.B">(Section III.B)</span>. The forecasts never come close to that: the largest relative gap between them in any month is 140 parts per million <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section III.B">(Section III.B)</span>. The median relative gap between the raw weight vectors is 0.607 <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table V">(Table V)</span>.

Nothing in the forecasts explains this. The paper asks what does. The answer turns on a quantity most research never mentions: the ruler. A factor model must decide what one unit of exposure means and when two exposures count as unrelated. IPCA, the standard model, uses a plain ruler on coefficient vectors, as if each of the 132 characteristics were an independent, equally scaled coordinate. QZ-IPCA uses a ruler built from the data, the characteristic Gram matrix, which records how much the 132 characteristics overlap across stocks <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section I.B">(Section I.B)</span>. The two models differ only in that ruler.

So the research question is this. Once a model has produced its forecast, how does characteristic geometry, meaning the scale and overlap of firm characteristics, change the portfolio an investor actually holds? <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Abstract; Introduction">(Abstract; Introduction.)</span>

Here is the mechanism in two sentences. The portfolio rule adds a small fixed safety penalty, 0.01, to every factor's risk, and it adds it in each model's own units. The two rulers give the factors different units, so the same 0.01 is a different penalty, and the rule responds to the penalty, not to the forecast <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section IV.B">(Section IV.B)</span>. Sections 5 and 7 show this in arithmetic and in the data. Section 8 adds a second finding the paper meets on the way.

::: {.stat}

:::
::: {.stat}
<span class="big">0.83</span> Portfolios: median weight cosine (interquartile range 0.753 to 0.878)
:::
:::

<div class="figcaption">Same forecast, different portfolio <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section III.B; Table V">(Section III.B; Table V)</span>.</div>

## Why it matters: three reasons, each with a number {#why-it-matters}

Because a forecast is not a portfolio, and almost all attention goes to forecasts. Every quantitative equity strategy has two steps. First, predict which stocks will do better. Second, turn the prediction into positions. The second step passes through a risk model, and a risk model has units. This paper shows that the units are part of the strategy.

**First, the puzzle above is measurable.** Two investors with identical forecasts can hold different books for reasons that have nothing to do with information. Comparing forecasts alone would miss this source of variation in holdings <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Introduction">(Introduction)</span>.

**Second, a signal is left out.** Factor models estimate an intercept: the part of expected return that characteristics predict but the factors do not explain. A portfolio built from the factor terms alone leaves it out <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section V.A">(Section V.A)</span>. Within one fitted NA-IPCA model, switching that intercept off gives a gross Sharpe ratio of 0.39; putting it back into expected returns gives 2.51 over 594 months <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table VII, Panel A">(Table VII, Panel A)</span>. Gross means before all trading, financing and borrowing costs, and the page repeats that wherever the number appears. One more thing shapes how to read it. How much of a stock's expected return lands in the intercept rather than in the factor terms is set by the ruler, not by the data alone <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section I.D">(Section I.D)</span>. So the number is the value of using one block of one decomposition, and Section 8 says what that block contains.

**Third, the characteristic library is crowded.** Across 618 months, the 132 characteristics behave like about 20: a statistic the paper calls the participation dimension, roughly the number of equal-sized directions it would take to carry the same spread of exposure, has a median of 19.8 <span class="loc" title="Working paper and its Internet Appendix, draft September 2026: Figure 1; Table IA.III">(Figure 1; Table IA.III)</span>. Most new signals re-describe old exposures. When most signals point at the same few exposures, the rule for measuring exposure decides how much of a forecast becomes a bet.

The durable lesson is smaller than any Sharpe ratio and more useful. Before you read a change in holdings as new information or a new risk, check the units and the regularisation <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section IV.C">(Section IV.C)</span>.

::: {.stat-row}
::: {.stat}
<span class="big">0.83</span> Identical forecasts, different books: median weight cosine <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section III.B; Table V">(Section III.B; Table V)</span>
:::
::: {.stat}
<span class="big">0.39 → 2.51</span> Gross Sharpe ratio, same fit, 594 months, before costs <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table VII">(Table VII)</span>
:::
::: {.stat}

## How the paper answers it: change one thing at a time {#how-the-paper-answers-it}

The design is a controlled comparison. Almost everything is held fixed and one thing changes at a time <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table II">(Table II)</span>.

**Data.** 132 stock characteristics from the @jensen2023replication panel for U.S. mega, large and small caps, micro-caps excluded. Each characteristic is rank-scaled every month: converted to its percentile rank among all stocks and shifted to run from minus 0.5 to plus 0.5 <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section II.A">(Section II.A)</span>. Every month the model is refitted on the previous 120 months and used to build a portfolio for the next month only. That gives 618 months in which a portfolio is built, from June 1973 to November 2024, with about 2,000 stocks a month <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section II.A">(Section II.A)</span>. A stricter 594-month sample from June 1975 is used whenever a rule needs 24 prior estimates of its loadings <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section II.B">(Section II.B)</span>.

**Models.** Three specifications share three latent factors and five observed Fama-French factors and differ only in the ruler and the intercept <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table I">(Table I)</span>. IPCA: plain ruler, no intercept. QZ-IPCA: Gram ruler, no intercept. NA-IPCA: Gram ruler plus a fitted intercept, kept below a size cap that in practice is never reached <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table I; Section II.A">(Table I; Section II.A)</span>. Because the cap is never reached, the estimated intercept is the same one an uncapped fit would produce. In this sample the cap names the specification and gives the intercept a unit of measurement; it does not change any estimate <span class="loc" title="Internet Appendix to the working paper, draft September 2026: Appendix IA.1.3">(Appendix IA.1.3)</span>. The paper's "no-arbitrage" label is therefore a statement of motivation, not of a restriction that shaped the results. The Gram ruler is built three ways inside each window: EWMA (an average that weights recent months more, with a 60-month half-life), an equal-weight 120-month average, and a rolling 60-month mean <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section II.B">(Section II.B)</span>. All three are reported; none is selected by significance. Two benchmarks run under the identical protocol: FF5 (the five Fama-French factors alone) and RP-PCA [a variant of principal components that also fits average returns, @lettau2020estimating]. An archived PCA (plain principal components) configuration is excluded because its forecast is degenerate, not as evidence against PCA <span class="loc" title="Working paper and its Internet Appendix, draft September 2026: Section II.C; Appendix IA.2.2">(Section II.C; Appendix IA.2.2)</span>.

**Portfolio rule.** One mean-variance rule for every model: the rule bets more where expected return is high and risk is low, so weights equal the inverse of a risk matrix times expected returns <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section I.F, equations 8 and 9">(Section I.F, equations 8 and 9)</span>. To keep the arithmetic stable it adds a small constant, 0.01, to every factor's risk and to every stock's risk; the paper calls this a ridge, and this page calls it the safety constant or the ridge, nothing else. That constant is the hinge of Sections 5 and 7. Each month the positions are scaled so that long plus short exposure equals one dollar <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: equation 10">(equation 10)</span>, so comparisons are about direction, not leverage. Performance is gross of costs; a cost proxy appears only as a sensitivity check <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section II.C">(Section II.C)</span>.

**Inference.** A paired moving-block bootstrap: the same 12-month blocks of history are resampled for both strategies, 10,000 times, with 24- and 60-month blocks as stress checks <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section II.D">(Section II.D)</span>. Three things a careful reader should know. Pointwise means each interval is a 95 percent statement about its own comparison; across the dozens of comparisons on this page, the chance that at least one excludes zero by luck is well above 5 percent, and no correction for that is applied. The bootstrap resamples realised monthly returns with the fitted models held fixed, so it measures sampling variation in the performance comparison, not uncertainty in the estimated loadings, the ruler, or the choices of ridge, window and factor count <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section II.D">(Section II.D)</span>. A Sharpe difference is the difference of the two strategies' Sharpe ratios recomputed in each resample, not the Sharpe ratio of the return difference, and mean tests recentre the paired difference at zero before resampling <span class="loc" title="Internet Appendix to the working paper, draft September 2026: Appendix IA.5.3">(Appendix IA.5.3)</span>.

Table II is the paper's own map from question to evidence. This page's logic map follows it, and each row below jumps to the section that carries the evidence.

## Where it sits: IPCA, the ruler, and a bounded intercept {#where-it-sits}

IPCA [@kelly2019characteristics] writes each stock's next-month excess return as its characteristics times a coefficient matrix, in three blocks: three latent factors the model discovers, five observed Fama-French factors, and an intercept that does not move with any factor <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section I.A, equation 1">(Section I.A, equation 1)</span>. Loadings, the sizes of a stock's bets on each factor, are not fixed numbers; they are weighted sums of the stock's 132 characteristics, so they move when the characteristics move. The data pin down only the sum of the three blocks, which the paper calls the complete fitted index. How that sum is split is a convention, and the ruler sets it.

IPCA measures a loading direction the way you would measure a list of numbers: square each entry and add. It treats each of the 132 characteristics as its own axis, all the same size and all at right angles. QZ-IPCA measures the same direction by the size of the bet it creates across stocks: a direction's squared length is the average squared exposure it generates in the cross-section, computed from the Gram matrix, the average across stocks of products of characteristics <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section I.B, equation 3">(Section I.B, equation 3)</span>. Under that ruler two directions count as unrelated only if the stocks they pick do not overlap. Several value measures and several momentum measures pick many of the same stocks, so the two rulers disagree. Two loading vectors can be perpendicular on paper and still buy the same stocks.

Proposition 1 <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section I.D">(Section I.D)</span> is the hinge. Switching ruler is a matched transformation. The latent loadings are re-based to unit length under the new ruler. Whatever part of the Fama-French loadings and the intercept overlaps with the latent directions moves into the latent block. The latent factor series is rescaled and shifted so that it carries exactly what moved <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: equation 6">(equation 6)</span>. Every fitted return and every residual comes out identical. Only the labels and the units change. Like quoting a salary in euros a month instead of dollars a year: every number on the page changes, and nothing about the job does. The general construction and its inference theory are in a companion paper, Characteristic-space metrics in factor models: identification and inference [@liu2026metrics]; this page states only the case the portfolio analysis needs <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section I.D; Section I.E">(Section I.D; Section I.E)</span>.

NA-IPCA adds one piece: a characteristic-driven intercept, kept orthogonal to the latent block under the ruler and capped by an exposure budget <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section I.C, equation 5; budget 0.035, Table I">(Section I.C, equation 5; budget 0.035, Table I)</span>. The name refers to bounding departures from a zero-intercept pricing benchmark. It is not a claim that the intercept is a pricing error, and reading it as mispricing would need a specified pricing benchmark <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section I.C">(Section I.C)</span>. Two more cautions. The intercept is orthogonal to the latent loadings in characteristic space, but the positions it adds to a portfolio can still carry factor exposure <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section V.A, equation 18">(Section V.A, equation 18)</span>, so its return is not a zero-beta return and not alpha after factors. And the budget caps the intercept's contribution relative to how much characteristic exposure a portfolio takes, not relative to its risk, so it is not a bound on a Sharpe ratio or on distance from a pricing kernel <span class="loc" title="Internet Appendix to the working paper, draft September 2026: Appendix IA.4.1">(Appendix IA.4.1)</span>. The budget is the one place where a ruler change can exclude a model rather than relabel it <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section I.D">(Section I.D)</span>; in this sample it never binds, so that possibility is not observed.

The ridge is the bridge to portfolios. The portfolio rule maximises expected return minus one half of estimated variance <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section I.F">(Section I.F)</span>. The ridge adds a charge to that objective: one half of 0.01 times the sum of squared factor exposures, plus the same charge on squared stock positions <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section IV.B, equation 14">(Section IV.B, equation 14)</span>. One way to read it: adding 0.01 to each factor variance treats every factor as riskier than its sample history by the same fixed amount in its own units. A charge written in units that change with the ruler is a different charge under each ruler. The stock-position charge is already ruler-proof, because a position in a stock means the same thing under any ruler; that is why the fix is to write the factor charge the same way. Everything else in the objective survives the change of ruler. The next section shows it in arithmetic.

<div class="dfigure-title"><strong>What survives a change of ruler.</strong> A matched change of ruler <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Proposition 1">(Proposition 1)</span> leaves the left column untouched and changes the right one.</div>

| Invariant under a matched change | Not invariant |
|---|---|
| Fitted returns and residuals <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section I.D">(Section I.D)</span> | The factor ridge as seen in stock space <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section IV.B, equation 13">(Section IV.B, equation 13)</span> |
| The stock forecast <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section IV.B, equation 12">(Section IV.B, equation 12)</span> | The factor means and the factor series themselves: they rescale <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: equation 6">(equation 6)</span> |

> The Gram metric measures overlap in the stock-level exposures generated by those characteristics. <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Conclusion">(Conclusion)</span>

## A simple example in two parts {#a-simple-example}

Two small calculations, using only the paper's algebra <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Sections I.B and IV.B">(Sections I.B and IV.B)</span>. No data are needed. The numbers are illustrative units, not estimates from the paper.

**Part 1: what the Gram ruler sees.** Suppose there were only two characteristics, book-to-market and earnings yield. Scale each so that its average squared value across stocks is 1, and suppose their average product across stocks is 0.9: most stocks that are cheap on one are cheap on the other. The Gram matrix records those averages: 1 and 1 on the diagonal, 0.9 off it <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: equation 3">(equation 3)</span>. The paper's rank-scaled characteristics have average squared value near one twelfth, which only changes the units. The Gram matrix records average products, not correlations: it is a second moment and equals a covariance only after centring <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section I.B">(Section I.B)</span>.

Now take two loading directions. Direction a scores a stock on both cheapness measures added together. Direction b scores one minus the other. Under the plain ruler both have the same length and sit at right angles. Under the Gram ruler the average squared score across stocks is, for a, (1 + 0.9 + 0.9 + 1) / 2 = 1.9, and for b, (1 minus 0.9 minus 0.9 + 1) / 2 = 0.1.

A stock that is cheap on both measures gets a big score from a and almost none from b. So a is a real bet and b is nearly nothing, even though the plain ruler calls them the same size. The Gram ruler sees that the two cheapness measures mostly buy the same stocks; the plain ruler does not. With 132 characteristics the paper finds that the eigenvalue mass of the ruler is spread over the equivalent of about 20 equal directions, a measure of overlap rather than a count of independent bets <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Figure 1, Panel A; Section III.A">(Figure 1, Panel A; Section III.A)</span>.

::: {.tbl-num}
| Two-characteristic Gram toy | Book-to-market | Earnings yield |
|---|---|---|
| Book-to-market | 1 | 0.9 |
| Earnings yield | 0.9 | 1 |
:::

<div class="figcaption">Direction a (both measures added): Gram length² = (1 + 0.9 + 0.9 + 1) / 2 = 1.9. Direction b (one minus the other): Gram length² = (1 − 0.9 − 0.9 + 1) / 2 = 0.1. Under the plain ruler both have length² = 1 <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section I.B, equation 3">(Section I.B, equation 3)</span>.</div>

**The bridge from overlap to units.** Switching to the Gram ruler re-bases each direction to length 1 under that ruler. Direction a, whose Gram length is the square root of 1.9, about 1.38, has its loadings divided by 1.38 and its factor multiplied by 1.38. Direction b, whose Gram length is the square root of 0.1, about 0.32, has its loadings multiplied by about 3.2. That is the change of units in Part 2, with k = 1.38 for a and k = 0.32 for b. A fixed ridge of 0.01 now charges the crowded direction about half as much (1 / 1.9) and the spread direction ten times as much (1 / 0.1). This is arithmetic, not a claim about which ruler is better.

**Part 2: what a fixed ridge does when units change.** Two stocks, two independent factors, each stock loading on one factor. Factor 1: monthly mean 0.01, variance 0.02. Stock 1's loading on it is 1. Stock 1's own variance is 0.01. The ridge is 0.01 on the factor and 0.01 on the stock <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section I.F">(Section I.F)</span>.

Stock 1, original units. Forecast: loading times factor mean, 1 × 0.01 = 0.01. Factor risk: loading squared times variance, 1 × 0.02 = 0.02. Ridge charge: ridge times loading squared, 0.01 × 1 = 0.01. Total risk entry: 0.02 + 0.01 + 0.01 + 0.01 = 0.05. Raw weight: forecast over risk, 0.01 / 0.05 = 0.20.

Now change units. Double the factor: mean 0.02, variance 0.08. Halve the loading: 0.5. Nothing about the stock or the market has changed. This is the same model in different units, which is exactly what a change of ruler does <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section IV.B, equation 12">(Section IV.B, equation 12)</span>.

Stock 1, doubled units. Forecast: 0.5 × 0.02 = 0.01, unchanged. Factor risk: 0.25 × 0.08 = 0.02, unchanged. Ridge charge: 0.01 × 0.25 = 0.0025, one quarter of before <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section IV.B, equations 13 and 14">(Section IV.B, equations 13 and 14)</span>. Total risk entry: 0.0425. Raw weight: 0.01 / 0.0425 = 0.235.

With one stock this would only rescale the position, and unit-gross scaling removes the rescaling. That is why the second stock is there. Stock 2 is identical to stock 1 but loads on factor 2, whose units did not change. Its weight stays 0.20 while stock 1's rose to 0.235, so the rule now holds relatively more of stock 1: after scaling to one dollar, the split moves from 50/50 to about 54/46. That relative shift is what survives unit-gross scaling and what Table V measures at full scale. Rescale factor 1 by 10 instead of 2 and its ridge charge falls to one hundredth. A ruler change rescales the latent factor coordinates all at once and mixes the observed-factor overlap into them (the five observed factors keep their units), and it stretches as well as rotates, so the penalty on each affected direction changes <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: equation 13">(equation 13)</span>.

Why does a charge this small move real portfolios? In any direction, the ridge matters in proportion to 0.01 divided by that factor's variance in its reported units. Here that ratio is one half. Where a factor's reported variance is small, the ridge is a large share of its risk, and a change of units moves it a lot. The paper does not report which factors sit where; Table V reports the net effect on the weights, and it is large.

The fix takes one line. Convert the ridge with the units: the transported ridge is 0.01 × 2² = 0.04, and 0.04 × 0.25 = 0.01 again, so stock 1's weight returns to 0.20 <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section IV.B, closing paragraph">(Section IV.B, closing paragraph)</span>. Or write the penalty directly in stock space, where units do not depend on the ruler. Convert the currency, convert the fee.[^half]

[^half]: A note for the specialist: the implemented objective halves the whole risk term, so the ridge enters equation 14 as one half of 0.01 times the squared factor exposure. The factor of one half applies equally before and after the change of units and does not affect the comparison.

<div class="dfigure-title"><strong>The worked example.</strong> Stock 1 under three conventions <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section IV.B">(Section IV.B)</span>.</div>

::: {.tbl-num}
| | Original units | Doubled units | Doubled units with transported ridge |
|---|---|---|---|
| Forecast | 0.01 | 0.01 | 0.01 |
| Factor risk | 0.02 | 0.02 | 0.02 |
| Ridge charge | 0.01 | 0.0025 | 0.01 |
| Raw weight of stock 1 | 0.20 | 0.235 | 0.20 |
| Share of stock 1 after unit-gross scaling | 50 percent | 54 percent | 50 percent |
:::

<div class="figcaption">Stock 2 loads on a factor whose units do not change and keeps raw weight 0.20 throughout. Forecast and unregularised risk survive a change of factor units; a fixed ridge does not, and the relative position shifts <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: equations 12 to 14">(equations 12 to 14)</span>.</div>

## What the paper finds, part 1: the ruler is concentrated, and the puzzle is real {#results-part-1}

{{< include /_includes/_exhibit-helpers.qmd >}}

Start with the ruler itself. If the 132 characteristics did not overlap, the Gram ruler would be the plain ruler and nothing on this page would happen. The overlap is what makes the two rulers disagree, so the paper measures it first. Each of the 618 portfolio months has its own Gram matrix, built from the trailing 120 months with a 60-month half-life <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section II.B">(Section II.B)</span>. How concentrated is that ruler, and how much does it move over fifty years?

::: {#figure-rolling-geometry .column-page .dfigure aria-labelledby="figure-rolling-geometry-title"}
<div class="dfigure-title" id="figure-rolling-geometry-title"><strong>Figure 2: The rolling ruler.</strong> One statistic of the monthly characteristic Gram matrix, June 1973 to November 2024 (618 months); the dashed line marks the sample median where one is reported.</div>

{{< include /research/_fig-rolling-geometry.qmd >}}

<noscript><img src="/assets/img/hero_geometry.png" alt="Characteristic ruler for March 2009 and the participation dimension of the rolling characteristic geometry, June 1973 to November 2024, NBER recessions shaded" style="width:100%"></noscript>

<div class="figcaption"><strong>How to read it.</strong> Overlap among 132 characteristic exposures, one Gram matrix per month. The participation dimension measures overlap, not the number of priced risks <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section III.A">(Section III.A)</span>. NBER bands are retrospective context. Over the 618 months the participation dimension has a median of 19.8 dimensions (range 17.4 to 22.6) and the top-eigenvalue share a median of 14.2 % (range 11.8 % to 15.2 %); the equal-eigenvalue benchmark of 132 sits far off the axis. Hover for the month and value. <span class="provenance">Source: <em>Characteristic Geometry and Portfolio Choice</em>, working paper (draft September 2026), Figure 1 and Table IA.III; research release 2026-09-09 (<code>Characteristic_Geometry_and_Portfolio_Choice_Research_Release_2026-09-09</code>), <code>02_Presentation/Source/data/rolling_geometry.csv</code> and <code>03_Replication/modules/business_cycles/nber_monthly.csv</code>; release not public, available on request.</span> <a href="/data/hero_geometry.json">Data</a> · <a href="/assets/img/hero_geometry.png">PNG</a></div>
:::

All 618 are full rank, but their eigenvalue mass is concentrated. The participation dimension has a median of 19.8 and never leaves the range 17.4 to 22.6 <span class="loc" title="Working paper and its Internet Appendix, draft September 2026: Figure 1, Panel A; Table IA.III">(Figure 1, Panel A; Table IA.III)</span>. The largest single direction carries a median 14.2 percent of the total <span class="loc" title="Internet Appendix to the working paper, draft September 2026: Table IA.III">(Table IA.III)</span>. The shape of the ruler moves slowly: the median month-to-month drift in eigenvalue shares is 0.063 percentage points and the maximum is 0.115 <span class="loc" title="Working paper and its Internet Appendix, draft September 2026: Figure 1, Panel B; Table IA.III">(Figure 1, Panel B; Table IA.III)</span>. One hundred and thirty-two characteristics behave like about twenty, in 1973 and in 2024.

Two readings must be kept apart. The participation dimension measures overlap in the exposures the characteristics generate. It does not estimate how many independent or priced risks exist <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section III.A">(Section III.A)</span>. The drift measures changes in slice sizes, not rotation of the directions themselves. And because preprocessing is redone in every window, the series mixes changes in the stock sample, the transformations and the true relationships <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section II.A">(Section II.A)</span>. The recession bands in the figure are context, not evidence of a recession response.

::: {.stat-row .two}
::: {.stat}
<span class="big">17.36 to 22.63</span> Participation dimension, 618 months <span class="loc" title="Internet Appendix to the working paper, draft September 2026: Table IA.III">(Table IA.III)</span>
:::
::: {.stat}
<span class="big">11.76 to 15.21 percent</span> Largest eigenvalue share, 618 months <span class="loc" title="Internet Appendix to the working paper, draft September 2026: Table IA.III">(Table IA.III)</span>
:::
:::

Now the puzzle in numbers. The two models are estimated separately, so Proposition 1's exact agreement is a benchmark, not a guarantee; the 4.7 parts per million is the check that the separate fits come as close to it as numerical tolerance allows <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section III.B">(Section III.B)</span>. The largest angle between the two models' latent factor spaces is 0.011 degrees <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section IV.A; Table V">(Section IV.A; Table V)</span>. Yet the weight cosine is 0.83 and the median relative gap in raw weights is 0.607 <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table V">(Table V)</span>.

Performance shifts too. On 618 months the gross Sharpe ratio is 0.64 for IPCA and 0.91, 0.85 and 1.00 for the three Gram-ruler constructions; the maximum drawdown, the worst peak-to-trough loss, improves from minus 34.6 percent to between minus 16.5 and minus 19.8 percent <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table III">(Table III)</span>. Point estimates show higher means and lower volatility for every Gram ruler, but neither the mean gain nor the volatility reduction is established on its own; only the rolling-60 Sharpe ratio, a ratio of the two, has a range of plausible values that excludes zero, 0.37 with a 95 percent interval from 0.02 to 0.68, and only with 12-month blocks <span class="loc" title="Working paper and its Internet Appendix, draft September 2026: Table IV; Section III.C; Table IA.VI">(Table IV; Section III.C; Table IA.VI)</span>. The Sharpe interval can exclude zero while the mean and volatility intervals both include it. The Sharpe ratio is a ratio, and across paired resamples its numerator and denominator move together, so its resampling distribution is tighter than either part's. The evidence is for a higher ratio of mean to volatility under this rule, not for a higher mean or a lower volatility on its own <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table IV; Section III.C">(Table IV; Section III.C)</span>. The paper reports all three constructions rather than the one that happens to be significant. Whether that gain belongs to the ruler or to the ridge measured in the ruler's units is exactly what the paper cannot settle, because ridge-free portfolios were never run <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section IV.C">(Section IV.C)</span>.

## What the paper finds, part 2: a fixed ridge in changed units is the culprit {#results-part-2}

Section IV does the detective work in four steps.

**Step one: split the gap exactly.** The difference between two mean-variance portfolios can be written, with no approximation, as one piece from different expected-return inputs and one piece from different risk matrices <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: equation 11">(equation 11)</span>. The mean piece is small next to the covariance piece, which points at the risk matrix <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table V">(Table V)</span>. The page does not quote a percentage for the mean channel because the two term norms are not additive shares <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table V note; Section IV.A">(Table V note; Section IV.A)</span>.

**Step two: find the one term that is not invariant.** Under a matched change of factor units, the forecast and the unregularised stock covariance are exactly preserved <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: equation 12">(equation 12)</span>. The one term that is not preserved is the fixed ridge of 0.01 on each factor variance. A general change of factor basis does not preserve it; only an orthogonal change would, and a change of ruler need not be orthogonal <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: equation 13">(equation 13)</span>.

**Step three: delete only that term.** Equation 12 holds by algebra for matched representations. The two models here were estimated separately, so nothing forces it to hold. That is what makes this step a test rather than a tautology: if the two fits were not the same model in different units, deleting the ridge would not make their weights agree. The paper removes the factor ridge from the stored risk matrices, holds forecasts, residual variances and the stock-level ridge fixed, and re-solves the rule in every one of the 618 months <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section IV.C">(Section IV.C)</span>. The median relative weight gap between IPCA and QZ-IPCA falls from 60.7 percent to about 4 in a million. The maximum falls from 89.5 percent to about 0.01 percent <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table V">(Table V)</span>. One minus the weight cosine falls from about 0.17 at the median to about 6 in a trillion, and sits near that floor in every month, recession or expansion <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Figure 2">(Figure 2)</span>. That they agree to a few parts in a million in every one of 618 months is the evidence that the fits are matched and that the ridge was the only input that was not.

**Step four: check the plumbing.** Rebuilding the factor covariances from the saved factor histories reproduces the stored matrices to within 2 × 10⁻¹⁵ across all 1,236 model-window matrices <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table V">(Table V)</span>. The same pattern appears when both models are started from a common initialisation <span class="loc" title="Internet Appendix to the working paper, draft September 2026: Table IA.I">(Table IA.I)</span>, which supports the ridge channel rather than a starting-value explanation.

This is a mechanism check. It shows that the ridge, held fixed while the factor units change, is why the weights differ. It does not compute the returns of ridge-free or transported-ridge portfolios, so it cannot say which convention would have earned more <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section IV.C">(Section IV.C)</span>. The constructive answer is to transport the ridge with the coordinates, or to specify the penalty in stock space <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section IV.B">(Section IV.B)</span>. Before reading a portfolio difference as new information or a new risk, check the units and the regularisation.

<div class="dfigure-title"><strong>Table V of the manuscript: before and after ridge removal.</strong> 618 months, June 1973 to November 2024; IPCA versus EWMA QZ-IPCA.</div>

> A penalty held fixed in factor coordinates can nevertheless change the stock positions selected by the investor. <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Conclusion">(Conclusion)</span>

## What the paper finds, part 3: what the retained intercept adds {#results-part-3}

The second finding sits inside one fitted NA-IPCA model. Table VII holds the fit fixed and switches inputs to the portfolio rule: intercept off, intercept in the mean only, and the complete rule, which also charges positions whose intercept signal has wobbled over the last 24 estimates. Because the estimated model is identical across the three, any difference comes from how the fit is used, not from a better fit.

Over 594 months the gross Sharpe ratio goes from 0.39 with the intercept off to 2.51 with it in the mean <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table VII, Panel A">(Table VII, Panel A)</span>. The gain is about 0.49 percentage points a month, 49 basis points, where a basis point is one hundredth of a percent, with a 95 percent interval that clears zero by a wide margin <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Panel B">(Panel B)</span>. The complete rule adds almost nothing to the mean and a little to the ratio through slightly lower volatility, taking the Sharpe ratio to 2.53 <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Panel B">(Panel B)</span>. Both increments keep their sign under 24- and 60-month blocks <span class="loc" title="Internet Appendix to the working paper, draft September 2026: Table IA.VI">(Table IA.VI)</span>. The gain is in the expected-return input. This is a long-short research portfolio of tiny positions in about two thousand stocks, rebalanced monthly and measured before all costs; it is a statement about the information in the fitted mean, not a fund you could buy.

<div class="figcaption">The intercept-off forecast has a rank correlation near zero with returns <span class="loc" title="Internet Appendix to the working paper, draft September 2026: Table IA.IV">(Table IA.IV)</span>. Intervals are 95 percent paired block-bootstrap intervals with 12-month blocks <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table VII, Panel B">(Table VII, Panel B)</span>.</div>

One fact keeps the size of that gain in proportion. The factor-only forecast of this same fit has no cross-sectional ordering power: its rank correlation with next-month returns is about minus 0.005, against 0.025 for IPCA <span class="loc" title="Internet Appendix to the working paper, draft September 2026: Table IA.IV">(Table IA.IV)</span>. Under this ruler, the decomposition has placed nearly all of the fit's ordering information in the intercept block. The ablation therefore measures how much of this fit's mean lives in that block, and where that mean lives depends on the ruler: a matched change of ruler moves part of it back into the factor block, so "intercept off" would remove a different amount <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section V.A">(Section V.A)</span>. The paper keeps a second comparison for that reason. Against strategies estimated on their own without an intercept, the complete rule's 2.53 stands beside 1.13 for the best QZ-IPCA ruler and 1.49 for RP-PCA <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table VIII">(Table VIII)</span>: a gain of about one to one and a half Sharpe points, not two.

The mean increment is positive in all four size universes over the full sample, with p-values adjusted for testing four universes at once all at or below 0.003 <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table VI">(Table VI)</span>. Over the recent 206 months from October 2007, every interval includes zero <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table VI">(Table VI)</span>. The complete rule's gross Sharpe falls across three consecutive 198-month blocks, from 3.97 to 3.03 to 1.13 <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section VI.C">(Section VI.C)</span>. No direct between-period test is reported.

| Universe | Full sample (594 months) | Recent period (206 months from October 2007) |
|---|---|---|
| Core | 0.488 [0.348, 0.634] | 0.202 [−0.071, 0.409] |
| Mega | 0.239 [0.105, 0.409] | 0.206 [−0.035, 0.507] |
| Large | 0.347 [0.194, 0.508] | 0.174 [−0.120, 0.389] |
| Small | 0.666 [0.487, 0.840] | 0.251 [−0.061, 0.464] |
:::

<div class="figcaption">Holm-adjusted p-values are at or below 0.003 for all four full-sample rows and 0.32 for all four recent rows; every recent interval crosses zero <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table VI">(Table VI)</span>.</div>

On the common 594-month sample of separately estimated strategies, the complete rule has the highest gross Sharpe ratio, the lowest volatility and the shallowest drawdown <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table VIII">(Table VIII)</span>. The intercept-off figure of 0.39 belongs to the within-fit ablation, not to a separately estimated model, and the page marks it as such. Three readings fit the evidence: a pricing error relative to these eight factors, a premium on a risk the eight factors miss, or a sample regularity that has weakened since 2007. The paper does not separate them, and a gross Sharpe ratio cannot.[^forecast-rank]

[^forecast-rank]: Forecast statistics do not rank like portfolios. RP-PCA ranks stocks best of all the forecasts, with the highest rank correlation with realised returns, yet has the lowest predictive R-squared, about minus 0.26, because it mis-scales return levels; it also has the best benchmark Sharpe, since a unit-gross mean-variance portfolio ignores the scale of a forecast <span class="loc" title="Working paper and its Internet Appendix, draft September 2026: Table IA.IV; Section VI.B">(Table IA.IV; Section VI.B)</span>. A forecast can help order stocks for investment while performing poorly as a prediction of return levels.

## How this compares with prior work {#how-this-compares}

In plain words, the contribution is two things: a check that any portfolio rule can be put through, does the rule impose the same stock-level penalty after an equivalent change of factor coordinates, and a measurement of one input's worth inside one fitted model. It is a representation check and a same-fit ablation, not a new estimator.

The forecasting question is in good hands. @kelly2019characteristics let characteristics drive time-varying factor loadings. @gu2020empirical showed that flexible machine-learning forecasts from many characteristics add investor value. @kelly2024virtue showed that models with more parameters than observations can forecast better, even with little shrinkage. @lettau2020estimating showed how to extract factors that respect expected returns rather than only variance. @kozak2020shrinking showed how to shrink a stochastic discount factor built from many characteristic portfolios toward its high-variance principal components. @jensen2023replication supplied the open data this paper uses.

This paper sits one step later, where a forecast becomes a portfolio. @jagannathan2003risk showed that a position constraint and covariance shrinkage, pulling noisy risk estimates toward a simpler target, are two faces of the same adjustment, so a constraint and a regulariser are two descriptions of one preference over positions. @ledoit2017nonlinear showed how to choose the shrinkage to improve out-of-sample portfolios. Together with @demiguel2009optimal and @kan2007optimal on estimation risk, that literature works in stock space <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Introduction">(Introduction)</span>. This paper adds a third description: in a factor model, a regulariser written in factor units is a preference that changes when the units do, so a normalisation choice that is harmless for fit enters the portfolio through the ridge <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section IV.B">(Section IV.B)</span>. In the author's words, the contribution is to connect characteristic-based return models to explicit choices in portfolio construction, so that the evidence separates differences in fitted models from differences in their use <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Introduction">(Introduction)</span>.

On the intercept, @kelly2019characteristics allow a characteristic-driven intercept and test whether it is zero, and @zaffaroni2025factor shows what asymptotic no-arbitrage implies for pricing errors in conditional models <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section I.C">(Section I.C)</span>. Principal Portfolios [@kelly2023principal] separates zero-beta from factor-exposed predictability; the retained intercept here asks a related but different question, what mean information remains after the declared factor blocks, and its portfolio value is not a zero-beta or arbitrage result.

Three works the draft does not yet cite are the closest neighbours. Universal Portfolio Shrinkage [@kelly2023universal] designs the shrinkage that maximises out-of-sample performance; this paper offers a representation check that any shrinkage rule could be put through, has not tested that method, and does not claim it fails the check. Machine Learning and the Implementable Efficient Frontier [@jensen2026implementable] shows that net-of-cost performance needs a cost-aware objective; this paper works upstream of costs and would be a natural input to such an objective. Principal Portfolios is the third, as above.

Three further contrasts help place the work. @demiguel2020transaction show that trading costs change which characteristics matter; this paper shows that the risk penalty changes which positions are taken, for a fixed set of characteristics. @brandt2009parametric never form a factor covariance, so the factor-ridge channel studied here has nowhere to enter; that is a strength of their design. @didisheim2024apt find that more factors help; this paper holds the factor count fixed and varies only the coordinates.

The contribution is narrow, and stated as such. A representation result <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Proposition 1">(Proposition 1)</span>, stated here as a special case of the companion paper on characteristic-space metrics [@liu2026metrics], which carries the identification and inference theory. An algebraic observation that a normalisation choice enters the objective through an otherwise fixed ridge, with a two-line remedy <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section IV.B">(Section IV.B)</span>. A stored-matrix experiment that confirms the channel month by month <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table V; Figure 2">(Table V; Figure 2)</span>. A same-fit ablation that isolates the investment value of the retained mean <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Table VII">(Table VII)</span>. And an explicit list of what is not established.

<div class="dfigure-title"><strong>Literature comparison.</strong> Rows marked † are the author's reading of works the current draft does not cite; they are offered as context, not as claims the paper makes. Each entry links to its reference, which carries the verified page.</div>

::: {.lit-table}
| Prior work | What it established | How this paper relates |
|---|---|---|
| @kelly2019characteristics, IPCA | Characteristics instrument time-varying factor loadings; characteristic return the factors do not explain goes to an intercept that is tested as a set of anomaly intercepts | Shows that the loading normalisation, harmless for fit, changes portfolios through a fixed ridge; measures the intercept's portfolio value within one fit rather than testing it as a pricing error |
| @zaffaroni2025factor, conditional factor pricing | Inference on pricing errors in conditional models with large cross-sections; asymptotic no-arbitrage implies summability of pricing errors rather than zero intercepts | Bounds the intercept's exposure and measures its portfolio value; states the conditions a pricing interpretation would need rather than asserting it |
| @jagannathan2003risk | A portfolio constraint is equivalent to covariance shrinkage | A factor ridge is equivalent to a stock-level exposure penalty whose form depends on the factor representation |
| @demiguel2009optimal | Estimation error can make optimised portfolios lose to equal weights; the case for regularising inputs | Here the regularisation is a factor ridge, and its stock-space effect depends on the factor units |
| @kan2007optimal | Optimal portfolio rules under parameter uncertainty | The instability penalty is a proxy for that uncertainty, not a calibrated version of it <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section V.B">(Section V.B)</span> |
| @ledoit2017nonlinear, nonlinear shrinkage | Covariance shrinkage with as many parameters as assets is optimal for portfolio selection | A factor-space ridge implies a stock-space adjustment that depends on factor units; recommends transporting it or specifying it in stock space |
| @brandt2009parametric, parametric portfolio policies | Model weights directly as functions of characteristics; no covariance needed | No factor covariance is formed, so the factor-ridge channel has nowhere to enter, which is a strength of their design; this paper covers methods that pass through a factor model |
| @lettau2020estimating, RP-PCA | Adding a pricing-error penalty to PCA recovers low-variance factors that matter for returns | Implemented here as an eight-factor benchmark on characteristic-managed returns (gross Sharpe 1.49 on 594 months, Table VIII; construction in Appendix IA.2.2); this paper varies the use of a model's output, not the factor estimator |
| @gu2020empirical, ML asset pricing | Nonlinear ML forecasts from many characteristics create large investor gains | With forecasts held almost exactly fixed, portfolios still differ; forecast accuracy and portfolio value answer different questions |
| @jensen2023replication, Replication crisis | Most factors replicate and cluster into 13 themes; open global characteristic data | Uses their data; measures overlap among 132 characteristic exposures (median participation dimension 19.8) as a descriptive statistic, not a count of priced risks |
| † @kelly2023principal, Principal Portfolios | Cross-security predictability decomposes into zero-beta alpha and factor-exposed beta strategies | A same-fit ablation of the retained intercept inside a mean-variance rule; claims no zero-beta or arbitrage result |
| † @jensen2026implementable, Implementable Efficient Frontier | Net-of-cost performance needs a cost-aware portfolio objective | An upstream design choice, the units of the exposure penalty, evaluated gross; a transported penalty plus a cost-aware objective is a proposed extension |
| † @kelly2023universal, Universal Portfolio Shrinkage | Nonlinear shrinkage that reweights return components to maximise out-of-sample performance | A representation-invariance check that any shrinkage rule could be put through; not applied to their method, and no claim that it fails |
| † @kozak2020shrinking, Shrinking the cross-section | Shrink SDF coefficients on low-variance principal components; robust out-of-sample SDF | The coordinate system in which a penalty is applied has portfolio consequences even when it was chosen for normalisation rather than for economics |
| † @demiguel2020transaction | Transaction costs raise the number of jointly useful characteristics because trades cancel | The risk penalty, not costs, changes positions for a fixed characteristic set; results are gross of costs |
| † @freyberger2020dissecting | Many characteristics are redundant; nonparametric selection improves prediction | Keeps all 132 characteristics and measures redundancy through the Gram metric used to normalise loadings |
| † @kelly2024virtue, virtue of complexity | Models with more parameters than observations forecast better; the benefit of complexity survives light shrinkage | Concerns the allocation ridge at fixed model size and its invariance to factor units, not the prediction ridge or model size |
| † @didisheim2024apt, APT or AIPT | Factor models with enormous factor counts price assets better out of sample | Holds the factor count fixed and varies only the coordinates; a coordinate change with no effect on fit can still change holdings |
:::

> The evidence separates differences in fitted models from differences in their use, allowing investors to evaluate the particular portfolio decision responsible for a change in holdings or performance. <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Introduction">(Introduction)</span>

## Why practitioners should care {#why-practitioners-should-care}

Risk-model conventions are usually treated as housekeeping. This paper says they are part of the strategy. Five situations, then a checklist.

**Same forecasts, different books.** Two desks license the same forecasts but run risk models that measure exposure in different units. Their optimisers disagree, most of all in the directions whose units differ most between the two risk models <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section IV.B">(Section IV.B)</span>. That is a units disagreement, not a forecasting disagreement. The remedy is to transport the ridge with the coordinates, or to specify the penalty in stock space <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section IV.B; Conclusion">(Section IV.B; Conclusion)</span>.

**Migration backtests.** A fund switches risk vendors and reruns its history. Month by month, identical forecasts now map to different weights, and turnover between the old and new books is a cost with no forecasting content. The paper's mechanism check says where such a gap can come from; it does not say which book earns more <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section IV.C">(Section IV.C)</span>.

**Crowding.** In August 2007 funds with different forecasts held nearly the same positions and unwound them together. Institutional Investor's [ten-year retrospective](https://www.institutionalinvestor.com/article/b1505psmpklytc/the-next-quant-meltdown) and its [2024 profile of AQR's three quant crises](https://www.institutionalinvestor.com/article/2dqsr456gmu55p19gxiio/corner-office/cliff-asness-has-steered-hedge-fund-aqr-through-not-one-not-two-but-three-quant-crises) both describe that episode as crowding. The paper's participation dimension measures overlap among characteristic exposures inside one model's library <span class="loc" title="Working paper and its Internet Appendix, draft September 2026: Figure 1; Table IA.III">(Figure 1; Table IA.III)</span>. That is a different object from crowding across funds, but it is a price-free complement to order-flow measures such as [Risk.net's 2020 study of factor crowding](https://www.risk.net/cutting-edge/investments/7711291/zooming-in-on-equity-factor-crowding).

**The factor zoo.** The "factor zoo" is the hundreds of published return predictors. Institutional Investor reported [in 2019](https://www.institutionalinvestor.com/article/2bswfy2zxil3sxfzd1pfk/portfolio/what-asset-managers-dont-want-you-to-know-about-their-factor-funds) that managers keep launching proprietary factors nobody outside has replicated, and [in 2020](https://www.institutionalinvestor.com/article/2bsx0rbbf950e3nq9dc74/portfolio/the-missing-piece-for-quants) that "pure", non-overlapping factors matter more than adding signals. Overlap is exactly what the Gram ruler records <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section I.B">(Section I.B)</span>. Before concluding that 30 new alternative-data signals are useless because the model's fit barely improves, ask how much of their exposure overlaps with the roughly 20 directions already covered. Overlap is what the Gram ruler records; it does not say how many priced risks there are <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section III.A">(Section III.A)</span>. That is the same scepticism practitioners voiced about [big data in 2017](https://www.institutionalinvestor.com/article/b1505q8nnxr58t/quants-skeptical-of-big-data-machine-learning-hype) and about [AI stock picks in 2026](https://www.institutionalinvestor.com/article/why-overrelying-ai-stock-picks-recipe-disaster).

**Backtest to live.** Institutional Investor's [2018 piece on momentum funds](https://www.institutionalinvestor.com/article/2bsxnp1o13l7lkonzdp8g/portfolio/the-momentum-factor-is-real-too-bad-it-doesnt-work) is a reminder that turnover eats paper Sharpe ratios. Every number on this page is gross. Figure 1's 0, 10 and 50 basis point views exist for that reason, and those lines are a proxy rather than a net return <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section VI.D">(Section VI.D)</span>. An asset owner comparing two backtests should hold the cost convention fixed, just as the paper holds the risk-model units fixed.

**Checklist: before you attribute a change in holdings to new information.**

1. Confirm the factor units. Has the loading normalisation or the risk-model metric changed?
2. Confirm the ridge was transported with the coordinates, or written directly in stock space <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section IV.B">(Section IV.B)</span>.
3. Compare forecasts and weights separately. Agreement in one does not imply agreement in the other <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section III.B">(Section III.B)</span>.
4. Hold the cost convention fixed across the backtests you compare <span class="loc" title="Working paper, draft September 2026: Section II.C">(Section II.C)</span>.
